title: Plan AO: AI PRD Writing
summary: Interviews → feature list → user stories → acceptance criteria → review iterations
scenario: For product managers who want to turn scattered ideas into an executable PRD quickly — grounded in interview notes, not generated from thin air.

steps.title: Collect interviews & inputs
steps.detail: Write user interview notes, feedback, competitor observations and stakeholder asks into Notion, tagging each as 'verified' or 'assumption'. With raw material in place, AI output won't drift.
steps.tips: For every requirement, capture who runs into what problem in which scenario — that's the raw material for user stories.

steps.title: Feature list
steps.detail: Have the model organize the material into a feature list: grouped by module, prioritized (P0/P1/P2), with dependencies and conflicting requirements removed. Align on 'what we build' before touching details.
steps.tips: Ask the model to score each feature on user value × build cost; keep only high-value, low-cost items in P0.

steps.title: User stories
steps.detail: For each P0/P1 feature, write a user story: 'As a <role>, I want <action>, so that <outcome>.' Have the model fill in edge cases and error flows to build story cards.
steps.tips: Give every story one happy path and two exception paths — that's ready-made input for dev and QA.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria
steps.detail: Turn user stories into testable conditions using 'when X happens, the system should Y', covering normal, edge and error cases, plus an explicit 'not a bug' list.
steps.tips: Write criteria well enough that QA can copy them directly; half an hour here saves days in development.

steps.title: Review & iterate
steps.detail: Lay the PRD out as a visual document in Gamma for team review, feed feedback back into Notion, and have AI update requirements and priorities into a v2 for another pass.
steps.tips: In review, debate only whether it serves target users — leave implementation arguments for the technical design stage.

pitfalls.title: Letting AI invent the whole PRD
pitfalls.detail: A PRD with no interviews or data is a castle in the air; feed material first, then let AI organize — reverse the order and you're just talking to yourself.

pitfalls.title: A feature list with no priorities
pitfalls.detail: All-P0 is no P0; rank by user value and cost. Cutting features protects delivery quality better than adding them.

pitfalls.title: Vague acceptance criteria
pitfalls.detail: 'Great UX' or 'fast' can't be tested; write concrete, testable conditions so QA has a verdict to apply.

pitfalls.title: Writing without reviewing
pitfalls.detail: A PRD that skips review breeds requirement drift during implementation; run at least one formal review before development.
